title: Spacing: forget a little, then pull it back
hook: The same study time spread over days beats one long session. Here's why, and how the recall checks are timed.

steps.prompt: From memory: what happens to something you learned if you never review it?
steps.answer: You forget most of it within days. Memory drops fast at first, then levels off (the forgetting curve).

steps.prompt: You have 3 hours to study circles for a test in two weeks. Which plan gives the best memory on test day?
choices: 1 hour today, 1 hour in 4 days, 1 hour in 10 days
steps.why: Same time, spread out. Spacing beats cramming for anything you need to remember for more than a day or two.

cards.text: Reread the chapter 5 times in a row
Mixed practice twice a week for a month

steps.why: Same total time, different results. Gaps between sessions make you work to remember, and that's what lasts.

steps.prompt: Why does waiting a bit before you review help?
choices: You've forgotten a little, so pulling it back takes effort, and that effort strengthens it
Your brain has to rest before it can store anything
It doesn't; reviewing right away is best
steps.why: Easy review feels good but does little. Effortful recall after a gap is what builds lasting memory.

steps.prompt: You finish a lesson on the 1st and pass each recall check on the day it's due. The gaps grow: 1 day, then 3, then 7.
steps.why: 5 + 7 = 12. Each successful recall makes the memory last longer, so the next gap can be longer.

steps.prompt: Interleaving means mixing problem types (slope, percents, circles) in one session instead of 20 of one kind. Why does it help on the SAT?
choices: The test mixes them, so you practice choosing the method, not just using it
steps.why: In a block of 20 slope problems you never decide what kind of problem it is. The SAT makes you decide every time.

steps.prompt: Jay's week of study. Tap the day that's cramming.
lines: Tue: a recall check on percents and a new lesson on ratios
Wed: a mixed set of 10 questions
Sat: 4 hours on the whole unit, the night before the test
steps.why: Four hours in one sitting right before the test feels productive, but most of it fades fast.

steps.prompt: Order a spaced plan for one new skill.
items: Day 1: learn it and do a few problems
Day 2: a quick recall check from memory
Day 5: mixed practice that includes it
steps.why: The gaps grow each time, just like the lesson recall checks.

keys: Spread the same study time out: spacing beats cramming.
Review when you've started to forget; the effort to remember is what helps.
Mix problem types so you practice choosing the method.

recall.prompt: Which plan is better for a test in two weeks?
choices: One long session the night before
recall.why: Spacing wins for anything you need to keep.

recall.prompt: Why does a gap before reviewing help?
choices: Recalling takes effort, and effort builds memory
recall.why: The struggle to pull it back is the point.

choices: Mixing different problem types in one session
recall.why: Mixing makes you choose the method, like the real test.

intro: Case file: Jay studied for 6 hours and forgot most of it by test day. Figure out what went wrong.
